item.title: Hong Kong's 1st five-year plan responds to public aspirations
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-20
Hong Kong's 1st five-year plan responds to public aspirations HONG KONG, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR)'s first five-year plan for economic and social development (2026-2030) released earlier this week turns the public's key everyday concerns into measurable, deliverable commitments to improve livelihoods across the city. The five-year plan and the 2026 policy address were both released on Sept. 16. The five-year plan sets out a blueprint for the future, and the policy address focuses on immediate priorities and actionable details. Housing is the top livelihood concern for Hong Kong residents. The plan clearly sets a public housing construction target of about 196,000 units over the next five years, while pledging to continuously optimize the home-ownership ladder and striving to largely eliminate substandard subdivided units in residential buildings by 2030. This proactive housing policy is widely seen as a shift in housing supply toward a "results-oriented" governance model, placing greater emphasis on tangible outcomes and real effectiveness. The Northern Metropolis is regarded as a new engine to resolve Hong Kong's deep-seated livelihood challenges in housing, employment, and youth development. The plan specifies a further upgrade for the Northern Metropolis University Town under the development concept of "One Town, Five Elements." By coordinating five key elements -- education, technology, industry, talent, and urban development, it aims to foster an innovation ecosystem deeply integrating industry, academia, and research. "Only by expanding space through development can improvements in people's livelihood have lasting momentum," said Holden Chow, a member of the Legislative Council of the HKSAR. Chow noted that this approach turns Hong Kong into a "super reservoir" for global talent and positions the Northern Metropolis as a strategic hub connecting the mainland and global markets. Ms. Lau, a Hong Kong resident who has waited three years for public rental housing and currently lives in a subdivided flat in Kowloon Bay, carefully flipped through the housing policy sections after receiving copies of the five-year plan and policy address. "Whether it is increasing the supply of Light Public Housing or eliminating substandard subdivided units, it gives me hope of moving into public housing sooner," she said. During the formulation of this inaugural five-year plan, the HKSAR government held a two-month public consultation, receiving over 17,000 views and suggestions across various sectors. Incorporating the public's voices into the top-level design ensures the policies align better with people's needs and sentiment. Quality healthcare is another livelihood priority. The five-year plan specifies that public hospital beds will increase to approximately 35,000 by 2031, and the cumulative number of beneficiaries of district health centers will reach 1 million within five years, charting a clear path to expand capacity and enhance quality. Hong Kong's healthcare reform places greater emphasis on "quality enhancement." By promoting all-round, high-quality, and high-standard development of traditional Chinese medicine, advancing the digital transformation of public hospitals, and optimizing medical talent cultivation, the primary healthcare network continues to be strengthened to deliver more continuous, convenient, and affordable healthcare. Young people are Hong Kong's future. The five-year plan establishes two dedicated youth sections, elevating youth development to a core position in governance. Ranging from expanding development space to supporting them in pursuing their dreams, the plan maps out systematic arrangements for their growth and success. Through a dedicated task force, Hong Kong will intensify promotion of its academic, scientific research, and international collaboration resources, highlighting both the "Study in Hong Kong" and "Study Tour in Hong Kong" brands. This not only provides quality educational choices for students from home and abroad, but also builds up youth momentum for Hong Kong's future. Judith Yu, chair of the Hong Kong Chamber of Commerce in China, said that by integrating education, talent, and youth development into a systematic framework, the five-year plan instills greater confidence in the future among all residents, especially the younger generation. Yu suggested that local industries establish lasting channels for local young people to integrate into and serve the overall national development through internships and engagement across diverse fields such as innovation and technology. item.title: China eyes strong cultural, tourism industries by 2030
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-20
China eyes strong cultural, tourism industries by 2030 BEIJING, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- China will strengthen its cultural industries and tourism over the next five years, aiming to steadily raise their share of GDP, according to the Ministry of Culture and Tourism. The 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for cultural and tourism development, newly released by the ministry, calls for turning the sectors into pillars of economic development and businesses that improve people's livelihoods and sense of happiness. One key target is 8.3 billion domestic trips a year by 2030, nearly 2 billion more than in 2025. Chinese tourists spent 6.3 trillion yuan (about 933 billion U.S. dollars) on domestic trips in 2025. The 2030 target is 7.7 trillion yuan. Market analysis shows tourism spending is increasingly flowing into sectors that blend culture and new experiences into travel. Traveling for concerts, sports events and commercial performances, or to explore places known for revolutionary history or modern industry, is a notable example. "It all points to the same trend: tourists are no longer satisfied with a tour that is just about moving from one place to another, but a trip that can invoke cultural identity, or enable them to express their identity or experience something new," said a report by Meadin Research Institute, a market analytics firm. Such an infusion represents a focus of efforts to boost cultural industry and tourism in the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for cultural and tourism development. The plan supports industrial tourism based on equipment manufacturing and consumer goods, travel packages featuring farming experiences, and comprehensive consumption scenarios. Other efforts include further integrating sports events with cultural tourism, fostering high-quality ski destinations and promoting deeper links between cultural tourism and transportation. For 2030, the plan pledges to create diverse, immersive and interactive consumption scenarios, while boosting spending on cruise and yacht tours and recreational vehicle camping. To cultivate tour packages and business models that integrate culture and tourism, the plan says revolutionary culture and fine traditional Chinese culture can be used to build an emotional connection and improve the tourist experience. It also encourages employers to ensure paid vacation and stagger holidays to boost tourism spending. GROWING APPEAL FOR INTERNATIONAL TOURISTS Improving tourist experience in China appeals to both domestic and international visitors, especially with continued support expected over the next five years. The World Tourism Cities Federation (WTCF) listed Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Hangzhou and Chengdu among the world's top 20 tourist cities in its latest World Tourism Cities Development Report (2025-2026). China has the most cities on the list, according to the report released at a sideline event during the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services, held in Beijing from Sept. 9 to 13. Joseph Lema, an expert with the WTCF, said competition among tourism cities has moved beyond attractions and visitor numbers. What matters now, he said, is the ability to deliver quality experiences, effective governance and sustainable development. On the way to building strong cultural and tourism industries, China is more confident in realizing its ambitious inbound tourism goal. In the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for cultural and tourism development, the target is to attract 190 million inbound tourist visits a year by 2030. To reach that goal, China will continue to make travel easier for international tourists in areas such as visa-free policy, payment, tax refund, accommodation and transportation. Easier access and more options, from hairstyling and dental care to traditional Chinese medicine and custom tailoring, will bring longer stays by overseas visitors. "This allows them to see a more authentic, diverse and vibrant side of China," said Hu Yang, senior vice president of Tujia. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: When AP says the US should thank China
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-20
When AP says the US should thank China Photo shows a 100MW tower-type solar thermal power plant in Amdo county, Nagqu, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region. (People's Daily Online/Wu Yuren) The world has China's "energy strategy to thank" for avoiding a "much worse" oil price shock. So wrote the Associated Press (AP) in a report on Saturday, saying that "we've been free-riding off Beijing in a weird way" and that the US should "thank" China. The lengthy report focused on the turmoil in global oil markets triggered by concerns over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. It argued that China's forward-looking energy planning has enabled the country to withstand the pressure while easing global demand, thereby softening the upward price effects for the US, Europe and other regions. At a time when much of the Western media is busy reviving the "China shock" narrative, this may be one of the more clear-eyed assessments of China to come from a mainstream US media outlet in quite some time. One of the two experts interviewed by the AP said China "deserves credit" because it "did in 10 years what took us 25 years after the 1973 oil crisis to do." The other saw it as a "vindication" of China's last five-year plan and focus on "self-reliance." Notably, neither expert has a pro-China background. One is retired US Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery, an analyst at the hawkish Washington think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies, while the other is Jonathan Czin, a former senior CIA analyst who now works at the Brookings Institution. What makes the report worth noting is not that it has suddenly "said something nice about China," but that it brings a question that has long been politicized back to the realm of common sense. China's oil stockpiling and efforts to reduce imports were first and foremost intended to safeguard its own energy security. But global markets are interconnected. At a time of tight global oil supplies, China did not scramble for oil but instead left more supply available to others, easing pressure on the market and putting a lid, at least to some extent, on the price hiking. The portion of the bill that the US, Europe and other importers therefore did not have to pay is simply the most basic arithmetic of interdependence. It is not difficult to work out. In fact, this is just one window into how China interacts with the world. Forward-looking planning serves China's own interests first, but in an interconnected world, it can also become a public good. China has helped move clean energy from the laboratory to mass production, turning solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles into scalable infrastructure. Developing countries can consequently electrify their grids, modernize transportation and reduce imported fuel bills at lower cost, while developed countries have faced less energy-driven inflationary pressure during periods of heightened price sensitivity. Advocates of the "China shock" narrative always like to portray China's capabilities as something that comes at the expense of others. But when crises hit, the world can clearly see that China has repeatedly helped make things "less bad." That also offers a more honest lens through which to view China-US relations. The relationship between the world's two largest economies is not a simple equation in which "your gain is my loss" or "what you have, I cannot have." What the two countries should guard against and avoid is not each other's development, but turning an interconnected world into a distorted zero-sum story. Whether or not Washington "thanks China," the essence of China-US economic and trade relations remains one of mutual benefit and win-win cooperation. That will not change. item.title: China's consumption shifts toward smart, health-related products: commerce ministry
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-20
China's consumption shifts toward smart, health-related products: commerce ministry BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's consumer market showed a stronger move toward smart, health-related and higher-quality products in the first eight months of 2026, with sales of smart glasses on major platforms surging 120 percent year on year, the Ministry of Commerce said on Sunday. Sales of electrocardiogram monitors jumped 75 percent during this period, while those of action cameras and organic food rose 26.9 percent and 7.4 percent, respectively, according to an official with the ministry. The latest breakdown offers a closer look at changes within China's consumer market after official data revealed that the combined retail sales of goods and services rose 2.5 percent year on year in the January-August period. Demand also remained robust for a range of consumption-upgrade products. Sales of communication equipment increased 16.3 percent, while cosmetics items registered growth of 6.1 percent, and sales of cultural products and office supplies were up by 6 percent. In contrast, sales of petroleum products fell 6.1 percent year on year in this period, which the official partly attributed to substitution by new-energy products. Services continued to outpace goods consumption. Retail sales of services expanded 4.9 percent in the first eight months of 2026, 3.9 percentage points faster than retail sales of goods. Demand for tourism consulting and rental services, as well as cultural, sports and leisure services, maintained relatively rapid growth during the summer holiday season, as Chinese consumers increasingly spent on services alongside physical goods, according to the official. Consumption growth also continued to spread beyond major cities. Rural retail sales of consumer goods reached 4.4 trillion yuan (about 651.65 billion U.S. dollars), up 2.3 percent year on year, and 1.3 percentage points faster than the growth recorded in urban areas. Boosting consumption remains a policy priority for China this year. In July, China unveiled a five-year plan for expanding consumption, outlining measures to upgrade both goods and services consumption and expand quality services in areas including catering, tourism, elderly care and healthcare. China has also expanded policy support for smart and energy-efficient consumption. Under its 2026 consumer goods trade-in program, backed by ultra-long special treasury bonds, subsidies cover automobiles, six categories of home appliances and four types of digital and smart products. Smart glasses were included among the nationally subsidized digital and smart products for 2026, with eligible purchases receiving subsidies of 15 percent of the sales price, capped at 500 yuan per item. item.title: China's Global Development Initiative gives Global South stronger voice, opportunities: former Egyptian PM
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-20
China's Global Development Initiative gives Global South stronger voice, opportunities: former Egyptian PM Former Egyptian Prime Minister Essam Sharaf addresses an event titled "Hong Ting Forum Cairo Dialogue: Chinese Modernization, Valuable Experience to the World" in Cairo, Egypt, on April 24, 2025. (Xinhua/Wang Dongzhen) CAIRO, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's Global Development Initiative (GDI) helps give developing countries, especially those in the Global South, a stronger voice in global governance while creating broader opportunities for development, former Egyptian Prime Minister Essam Sharaf has said. "After decades of major economic and social transformation, China has accumulated considerable development experience and become more willing to share this experience and its capabilities with other countries, especially those of the Global South," Sharaf, founder and chairman of the Sharaf Foundation for Sustainable Development, told Xinhua in a recent interview. Sharaf said one of the GDI's most important contributions over the past five years has been to bring development back to "the heart of global attention" at a time of geopolitical conflicts, economic competition and successive crises. "Development should not become a victim of these conflicts, but should remain a shared priority for the international community," he stressed, noting that peace and development are closely intertwined. Sharaf said sustainable peace is difficult to build in a world where development gaps are widening, just as real development is difficult to achieve amid conflict and instability. "One of the most important lessons reinforced by the initiative is that investing in development is, at the same time, an investment in stability, peace and the future," he said. Sharaf said the GDI also reflects a broader understanding of development that goes beyond economic growth and new projects to improve people's livelihood, reduce poverty, ensure access to food and energy, and strengthen health, education and resilience to crises. Turning to global governance, Sharaf said the GDI contributes to strengthening multilateralism by promoting greater participation of developing countries in international decision-making. "From this perspective, I believe the GDI makes an important contribution to shifting from the concept of governance for countries to a broader concept of governance with the participation of countries," Sharaf said. He said that the GDI's emphasis on participation is particularly important because major global challenges, from climate change and food security to energy and digital transformation, cannot be addressed by any single country alone. "Ultimately, true multilateralism is not simply about having a large number of countries around one table; it is about ensuring that everyone feels they have a voice, and that their interests and needs are part of the process of shaping a shared future," Sharaf said. He expected the digital sphere to be one of the most important areas for the GDI's future development, as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly central to one of the fastest technological transformations in human history. Sharaf warned that if advanced technologies are available only to wealthier countries and societies, the world could move from the traditional development gap to an even more dangerous digital divide. He said supporting the "Digital South" should go beyond expanding internet access and digital infrastructure to include building human capacity, transferring knowledge, strengthening digital education and scientific research, and ensuring equitable access to technology. Sharaf said the GDI can play an important role in linking digital development with equitable development, while helping ensure that developing countries benefit from advances in artificial intelligence. He also pointed to the China-led establishment of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, saying it aims to strengthen international cooperation and global AI governance while promoting the safe, equitable and inclusive development and use of artificial intelligence. "I believe the GDI has a major opportunity to help shape an important principle for the next phase: the future of technology should not be a future for a limited number of countries, but a shared future for humanity," he said. item.description:

Autumn colors transform landscape in Huma county, NE China's Heilongjiang Province Photo shows a stunning autumn view of Huma county, nestled at the eastern foot of the Greater Khingan Mountains in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province. Autumn sets the Greater Khingan Mountains ablaze with color, and Huma county — nestled at the eastern foot of the range in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province — offers spectacular views of its forests and waterways. In Oupu township, the mountains are covered in vibrant autumn foliage. Red, gold, and green leaves form layers of color across the hills, a striking contrast against the deep green of the forest. The clear, winding river that runs through the valleys reflects the colorful hills along its banks, bringing the autumn scenery of the mountains and water together. As breezes move through the forest, the changing light and swaying leaves add movement to the vivid landscape. item.title: From Tehran to Aichi-Nagoya, 52 years of China's rise through Asian Games
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-20
From Tehran to Aichi-Nagoya, 52 years of China's rise through Asian Games This file photo shows torchbearer Wang Shun and a digital torchbearer jointly lighting the cauldron during the opening ceremony of the 19th Asian Games in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, Sept. 23, 2023. (Xinhua/Cheng Tingting) * The 20th Asian Games officially opened on Saturday, offering an opportunity to look back on the transformation of Chinese sport over more than half a century. * China made its Asian Games debut in Tehran in 1974 and hosted the Asian Games for the first time 16 years later. Since then, China has topped the Asian Games gold medal table at 11 consecutive editions and hosted the event three times. * The Asian Games have reflected China's rise in international sport alongside its broader economic and social transformation. NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- The 20th Asian Games officially opened on Saturday night, offering an opportunity to look back on another remarkable journey: the transformation of Chinese sport over more than half a century. China made its Asian Games debut in Tehran in 1974. 16 years later, Beijing welcomed Asia to the Chinese capital as host of the 1990 Asian Games. Since then, China has topped the Asian Games gold medal table at 11 consecutive editions and hosted the event three times. For China, the Asian Games have come to represent far more than competition, reflecting the country's rise in international sport alongside its broader economic and social transformation. MAKING A DEBUT Zhang Dawei still remembers the autumn day in 1974 when, at the age of 28, the basketball player was given the honor of carrying the Chinese flag at the opening ceremony of the Asian Games in Tehran. "I blocked out everything around me," Zhang later recalled. "All I could think about was holding the flag properly and keeping pace with the team." This file photo shows Chinese athletes at the closing ceremony of the 7th Asian Games in Tehran, Iran, on Sept. 16, 1974. (Xinhua) For China, the moment carried significance far beyond sport. The country had been largely absent from international competition for more than a decade. The arrival of the Chinese delegation at Tehran airport attracted considerable attention, with photographs of the team appearing in newspapers in several countries the following day. The athletes soon gave the world another reason to take notice. Su Zhibo won the first gold medal of the Games in the men's free pistol event, while teammate Li Yamin set a world record in the women's 25-meter standard pistol competition. China finished third in the medal table with 33 gold medals. This file photo shows Su Zhibo posing for a photo at the shooting venue of the 7th Asian Games held in Tehran, Iran in 1974. Su won the men's 50-meter pistol event, becoming China's first Asian Games gold medalist. (Xinhua) The message was clear: China was returning to the international sporting community. In 1979, China's legitimate seat in the International Olympic Committee was restored, paving the way for Chinese athletes to compete more widely on the world stage. At the 1982 Asian Games in New Delhi, China won 61 gold medals, overtaking Japan, which had dominated the Asian medal table for years. It was the first time China had finished atop the standings, a position it has retained at every edition since. Among the rising stars in New Delhi was 19-year-old gymnast Li Ning, who won four gold medals. He would go on to become one of China's most recognizable athletes and, later, one of its best-known sports entrepreneurs. Looking back, Li said athletes of his generation understood that they carried a responsibility beyond competition. "China had just begun opening its doors," he recalled. "When athletes went abroad, we weren't simply going there to compete. We were also representing the image of our country." A WINDOW ON CHINA In 1983, China submitted its bid to host the 11th Asian Games in Beijing. Hiroshima, Japan, also entered the race, but Beijing ultimately won the bid. Securing the hosting rights was only the beginning. The organizing committee faced a funding gap of around 600 million yuan (89.45 million U.S. dollars). Then, a little girl named Yan Haixia donated 1.6 yuan (about 0.24 U.S. dollars) from her New Year's gift money to the organizers, helping spark a nationwide fundraising campaign. Between 1987 and 1990, people across China donated a total of 270 million yuan to help finance the Games, which is the first major international multi-sport event happened in the country. This file photo shows the opening ceremony of the 11th Asian Games in Beijing, Sept. 22, 1990. (Xinhua) After retiring from competition, Li Ning turned his attention to business. One of his ambitions was simple: Chinese athletes should be able to stand on international podiums wearing brands produced in their own country. The Li Ning Company sponsored clothing for the Asian Games torch relay and the Chinese delegation's medal ceremonies. The brand's appearance at the Beijing Games proved a landmark moment for China's emerging sportswear industry. On home soil, China's athletes dominated, winning 183 gold medals, nearly twice as many as South Korea and Japan combined. Yet the significance of the Beijing Games went beyond the medal table. At the closing ceremony, the Saudi Arabian delegation unfurled a banner reading "Thank you, China," while Bangladesh's read "Long live friendship." 18 years later, the symbolism of the Beijing Asian Games returned on an even larger stage. On the evening of Aug. 8, 2008, billions of viewers around the world watched as the Beijing Olympic Games opened with a spectacular ceremony. A series of giant footprints made from fireworks appeared to move along Beijing's central axis toward the National Stadium, better known as the "Bird's Nest." That same north-south axis had been transformed by the 1990 Asian Games. Two years later, the Asian Games returned to China, this time in Guangzhou. The context had changed dramatically. China had overtaken Japan to become the world's second-largest economy. Guangzhou's GDP had surpassed 900 billion yuan in 2009, more than half of China's entire national GDP in 1989. The contrast with Beijing 20 years earlier was striking. The 1990 Games had required a nationwide fundraising effort, while Guangzhou was able to rely largely on the resources of a single city and market-based financing to prepare for an even larger event. "Through a city's new path of development, people can see the spirit of reform taking shape across the country and experience the fruits of opening up," said Lin Yanfen, then an official with the Guangzhou Asian Games Organizing Committee. China's athletes once again dominated the medal table, winning 199 gold medals. But public perceptions of sporting success were beginning to change. Sport was increasingly becoming something to participate in and enjoy, rather than simply something to win. With Aug. 8 being designated National Fitness Day and the implementation of national fitness regulations, more Chinese people have been shifting from "watching sport" to "doing sport." 13 years later, Hangzhou took up the baton. This file photo shows the opening ceremony of the 19th Asian Games in Hangzhou, Sept. 23, 2023. (Xinhua/Chen Yichen) China's athletes remained the overwhelming force at the 2023 Asian Games, winning 201 gold medals, an Asian Games record for a single delegation, and topping the gold medal table for the 11th consecutive time. Technology became one of the defining features of the Hangzhou Games, with artificial intelligence, augmented reality and other digital tools integrated into the event. This file photo shows China's Cui Chenxi celebrating after winning the skateboarding women's street at the 19th Asian Games in Hangzhou, Sept. 27, 2023. (Xinhua/Pan Yulong) The Games also introduced the first digital torchbearer program. More than 100 million people joined the online torch relay, extending the Games' reach beyond the host city. From China's return to the Asian Games in Tehran in 1974 to the technologically advanced spectacle in Hangzhou, the country's Asian Games journey has traced more than five decades of change.
